in_text_mentions: Generally, DTs have a chronic progression, remaining asymptomatic for a long time and developing into a solid lesion which might present with pain. However, larger lesions and those adjacent to neurovascular structures may be associated with pain and functional impairment [1,2,3]. Desmoid tumor complications correlate to their locally aggressive character, causing compression and/or invasion of the adjacent organs and tissues (Figure 1). Intra-abdominal DTs may determine bleeding, intestinal obstruction, perforation and, infrequently, an abscess [1,2,3].

in_text_mentions: er abdominal pain for several months duration. Her pain was cyclical and worse around her menses. She had a previous surgical history of caesarian section 8 years prior and previous gastric bypass for morbid obesity. On physical examination, a moderate sized mass was present above her Pfannenstiel incision on the right abdominal wall that was firm in nature. Cross-sectional imaging demonstrated a right rectus sheath mass measuring 8 cm, which was well circumscribed and suspicious for a desmoid tumor (Figure 1). There was invasion of the fundus of the uterus (Figure 2). Surgery was recommended.

in_text_mentions: Radical resection of the affected abdominal wall musculature down to the peritoneum was performed to include a peripheral margin of 3 cm of healthy tissue. The defect was reconstructed with polypropylene mesh. Macroscopically, the lesion had a firm, gritty texture. On the cut surface, it was glistening white and coarsely trabeculated, resembling scar tissue (Figure 3). The histologic diagnosis was of desmoid tumor (Figure 4).

panels.figure_caption: Histological examination of the lesion stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) (original maginification x40). in_text_mentions: The histopathological report describes a lipomatous mass measuring 10 x 9 x 3.5 cm, within which 16 lymph nodes were found showing fatty degeneration and no neoplastic infiltration. The mass is composed of spindle cells with low cellularity, no atypia, and a myxoid stroma with sclerotic areas (Figures 5, 6).

in_text_mentions: le, measuring 9.1×6.3×8.2 cm. A trucut needle biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of desmoid-type fibromatosis. in_text_mentions: The patient and his family were seen the next day in the clinic to discuss the MRI results. The most appropriate next step was to set him up for a CT-guided biopsy of the mass since it was greater than 5 cm. Two specimens were obtained; one came from the anterior compartment of the thigh and the other from the posterior. Hematoxylin and eosin stain histology revealed bland spindle cell proliferation with abundant collagen and minimal atypia, as seen in Figure 5.

in_text_mentions: general condition was fair and he had a huge ulcerated anterior abdominal wall mass with everted edges measuring 16 cm × 20 cm (figure 1) which was reported as desmoid tumor after incisional biopsy was done. An abdominal CT scan showed hepatomegaly and a mass measuring 16 cm × 15 cm × 4.6 cm confined to the anterior abdominal wall with an intra-abdominal extension but no involvement of intra abdominal organs (figure 2). Neither genetic testing for the Adenomatous Polyposis Coli (APC) gene mutation nor screening with colonoscopy for adenomatous polyposis coli or colorectal cancer was performed.

in_text_mentions: but lack hyperchromasia. Intra-abdominal desmoids can sometimes contain relatively scanty collagen and a pronounced myxoid matrix. Spindle cells and collagen fibrils are usually arranged in ill-defined fascicles and interlacing bundles (Figs. 3, 4). Occasionally extensive glassy hyalinization, which is also a feature of keloid, may also be encountered. The tumors can vary in cellularity and may assume a more storiform architecture as well. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Real patient sagittal MRI from a case report of locally aggressive desmoid-type fibromatosis involving the lower lumbar spine; caption supports a soft-tissue mass with destructive changes and mass effect. B: Real patient pelvic MRI showing the large right retroperitoneal multilobulated desmoid mass; caption directly attributes it to locally aggressive desmoid-type fibromatosis. C: Real patient sagittal pelvic/lumbosacral MRI showing extent of the desmoid mass with L5 and L4 vertebral involvement; caption supports locally aggressive desmoid-type fibromatosis. D: Real patient sagittal pelvic/lumbosacral MRI showing extent of the desmoid mass with L5 and L4 vertebral involvement; caption supports locally aggressive desmoid-type fibromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: AlAnsari et al. Locally Aggressive Desmoid Tumor With L4-L5 Vertebral Invasion and Progressive Neurological Deficit: A Case Report.. Clinical case reports 2026. doi:10.1002/ccr3.73181. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbosacral spine and pelvis demonstrating locally aggressive desmoid‐type fibromatosis. (A) Sagittal lumbar MRI shows involvement of the lower lumbar spine with destructive changes centered around L4–L5/L5 and associated mass effect. (B) Pelvic MRI demonstrates a large right retroperitoneal multilobulated soft‐tissue mass extending toward the right pelvis/hip region. (C, D) Additional sagittal pelvic/lumbosacral images show the extent of the mass, with invasion and partial destruction of the L5 vertebral body and involvement of the right aspect of L4. The imaging findings explain the patient's severe lumbosacral pain, progressive right lower‐limb neurological deficit, and spinal instability.
in_text_mentions: exact interval between the two imaging studies was not fully documented in the available records, this change was interpreted as clinically significant enlargement during the symptomatic period. The mass extended into the lumbosacral region, completely invaded and partially destroyed the L5 vertebral body, and partially invaded and destroyed the right aspect of the L4 vertebral body. The destructive osseous involvement and mass effect correlated with the patient's severe lumbosacral pain, right L4/L5 sensory deficit, progressive right lower‐limb weakness, and mechanical instability (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (Beta-catenin, Desmin). Beta-catenin: Immunohistochemistry of a pelvic desmoid tumor showing spindle-shaped neoplastic cells with positive nuclear beta-catenin staining, a classic diagnostic finding; caption states positive aberrant nuclear beta-catenin. Desmin: Same tumor stained for desmin, showing negative staining in the spindle cell proliferation with internal positive control in vessels/muscle; caption states neoplastic cells were negative for desmin, supporting the diagnosis by exclusion.
panels.attribution_text: Ormonde et al. Pelvic Desmoid Tumor: A Rare Case with Difficult Diagnosis and Treatment.. Case reports in obstetrics and gynecology 2022. doi:10.1155/2022/7653246. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: The neoplastic cells expressed positive aberrant nuclear staining for beta-catenin and were negative for desmin.
in_text_mentions: There were no mitoses or necrosis observed. The excision was incomplete, with focal positive surgical margins. An extensive panel of immunohistochemistry was performed. The neoplastic cells stained negative for Cytokeratins, S100, SMA, desmin, STAT6, CD34, and DOG1 and expressed positivity for ϐ-catenin (nuclear expression), favouring the diagnosis of fibromatosis (Figure 4). Due to the rarity of the diagnosis and the distinct treatment implications of such diagnosis, the case was sent for a second opinion to a national expertise pathologist of mesenchymal tumors that supported the diagnosis.

B: High-power H&E from the same pre-operative incisional biopsy shows bland elongated spindle cells with vesicular nuclei, characteristic of desmoid-type fibromatosis. C: IHC stain from the same desmoid tumor biopsy shows spindle cells with patchy alpha smooth muscle actin expression, a supportive but not entirely specific finding in the context of the article. D: IHC stain from the same desmoid tumor biopsy shows patchy nuclear beta-catenin expression, a characteristic finding of desmoid-type fibromatosis.

in_text_mentions: ough and braided, mostly indistinguishable from the surrounding fibrous adipocytes. Microscopically, it consisted mainly of fibroblasts and fibrocytes, collagen fibers interspersed among them. The tumor cells exhibited spindle-shaped, fascicular, mat-like striate, or reticular bundle arrangements. The cellular morphology was benign, with inconspicuous nucleoli and rare nuclear mitosis. Interstitial vessels were abundant with focal bleeding and local mucoid degeneration. A large amount of collagen deposition was seen in the interstitium, and lymphocyte infiltration was seen around it (Fig. 2A).

Tumor cells were positive for β-catenin in 12 cases, SMA in seven cases, Vimentin in four cases, and Ki-67 proliferation index was 2%-20% (Fig. 2B, C, D). Desmin (4/11), S-100 (2/12), SOX10 (1/6), STAT6 (1/7), CD34 (1/12) were positive in a subset of cases. Notably, CD117 was absent in all cases. Additionally, molecular pathologic tests were conducted in three of the 12 cases, and CTNNB1 gene mutations were detected in two of them (Table 2).

axial T1 weighted post-contrast image; visual heterogeneous enhancement

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: Axial T1 post-contrast MRI shows a large right shoulder desmoid tumor with enhancement, consistent with extra-abdominal desmoid fibromatosis. B: Axial PD-weighted MRI during cryoablation shows the treated desmoid tumor; included as patient imaging but less specific for a diagnostic manifestation. C: Follow-up axial T1 post-contrast MRI shows residual desmoid disease along the chest wall with enhancement. D: Follow-up axial T2 fat-suppressed MRI shows residual desmoid disease along the chest wall. E: Annotated post-contrast MRI (overlay on C) shows enhancing desmoid tissue with linear non-nodular morphology. F: Annotated T2 fat-suppressed MRI (overlay on D) shows desmoid tissue with intermediate T2 signal and adjacent post-ablation T2 hyperintensity.
panels.attribution_text: Düx et al. MRI features that predict progression of residual disease after ablation of extra-abdominal desmoid fibromatosis.. European radiology 2025. doi:10.1007/s00330-024-11319-w. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: MR-guided cryoablation and post-ablation MRI features in follow-up MRI. A Desmoid tumor in the right shoulder of a 30-year-old female (14 × 9 × 12 cm), causing significant pain and limiting motion of the scapula (axial T1 weighted post-contrast image). B Cryoablation: Treatment of the tumor, which included a pullback and second round of treatment (Axial PD weighted images). C, D Residual disease (dashed arrows) along the chest wall measuring 4.5 cm in follow-up MRI 263 days following cryoablation (axial T1 weighted SPGR post-contrast (C) and axial T2 weighted SSFSE with fat suppression images (D)). E, F Key post-ablation imaging features used in the paper, with contours overlaid on images C and D. The dotted outline shows desmoid tissue that has intermediate T2 signal [+iT2] and enhances [+ENH], but appears linear and not nodular [−NOD]. The dashed outline filled with a pattern shows an example of an area of marked (fluid-like) T2 hyperintense areas that was attributed to post-ablation changes and not considered +iT2 signal. The arrows point to a region that only exhibits +ENH. Examples of nodularity [+NOD] are shown in later figures

in_text_mentions: ent, leading to the commencement of tamoxifen and oral etodolac, an NSAID. Despite this medical therapy, the tumor continued to grow and became symptomatic with pain, ultimately reaching a size of 87 mm in the axial image (Fig. 1). During this period, 10 months before surgery, the patient also underwent ESD for a duodenal adenoma. Additionally, 6 months before surgery, ERCP was performed for a gallbladder stone. Due to the tumor’s progression and symptoms, he subsequently underwent a less invasive resection, which prioritized function over achieving wide, microscopically negative (R0) margins.

infiltrated by collagen

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Preoperative biopsy histology shows bland spindle cells and collagen infiltrating fat and skeletal muscle, consistent with desmoid-type fibromatosis. b: Low-power surgical specimen histology demonstrates a spindle cell process infiltrating skeletal muscle and reaching the surgical margin, consistent with desmoid-type fibromatosis. c: High-power histology shows haphazard collagen bundles and bland spindle cells without mitoses or necrosis, characteristic of desmoid-type fibromatosis. d: Beta-catenin immunostain shows diffusely positive tumor nuclei, a characteristic immunohistochemical finding in desmoid-type fibromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: Dalit et al. Congenital desmoid tumor of the cheek: a clinicopathological case report.. Eplasty 2009. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 3.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic findings in desmoid type fibromatosis. (a) Preoperative biopsy specimen shows a mixture of adipose tissue and skeletal muscle infiltrated by collagen and bland round to spindle cells (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification × 100). Findings from the surgical specimen (b-d). (b) Low-power magnification shows a spindle cell process infiltrating skeletal muscle (bottom left) and reaching the blue-inked surgical margin (top right) (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification × 50). (c) High-power magnification shows a haphazardly arranged collagen bundles and spindle cells with round to oval nuclei. No mitotic figures and no necrosis seen (hematoxylin and eosin, original magnification × 200). (d) β-Catenin immunostain shows diffusely positive staining in tumor nuclei (immunoperoxidase, original magnification × 200).
in_text_mentions: The previous biopsy was reexamined, and the histopathological analysis was found to be compatible with an invading edge of fibromatosis (Fig 3).

in_text_mentions: An ultrasound examination was performed and demonstrated a large mass of heterogeneous echogenicity with smooth, sharply defined margins in the left anterolateral abdominal wall (Figure 1). Preoperative CT scan images revealed a well-circumscribed, large mass (9 × 8 × 6 cm) of attenuation equal to that of muscle. The mass originated from the left rectus abdominis muscle and after intravenous administration of contrast medium demonstrated mild enhancement even in the delayed images. No pathologic adenopathy was present (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: H&E histology panel from a desmoid tumor case showing bland spindled to stellate cells in collagenous stroma. B: Higher-power H&E histology of desmoid tumor with collagenous stroma, focal myxoid change, and low mitotic activity; caption annotations present.
panels.attribution_text: Elhaddad et al. A Giant Sporadic Intra-abdominal Desmoid Tumor in a Male Patient: A Case Report.. Cureus 2022. doi:10.7759/cureus.26633. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 4.
panels.figure_caption: Histology (hematoxylin and eosin stain) (A) The tumor was composed of uniform, bland spindled to stellate cells with low cellularity. (B) The stroma was collagenous with occasional myxoid changes (arrow). No necrosis and hemorrhage were identified. Mitosis is <1/10 HPF (arrowhead).
in_text_mentions: Histopathology showed low cellularity composing of uniform bland of spindled to stellate tumor cells with small vesicular nuclei. These cells contained several tiny nucleoli and low mitoses (<1/10 HPFs). No tumor necrosis and hemorrhage were identified. Stroma was collagenous with occasional myxoid changes (Figure 4). These findings were consistent with the diagnosis of a benign desmoid tumor. The vermiform appendix, colon, and ileum were unremarkable upon examination.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: H&E low-power micrograph of the patient's desmoid-type fibromatosis showing long intersecting fascicles of bland spindle cells in a dense collagenous stroma, matching the captioned histopathology. B: Higher-magnification H&E micrograph of the same desmoid-type fibromatosis, showing cytologically bland spindle cells with elongated nuclei, as captioned. C: Immunohistochemical micrograph showing strong nuclear and cytoplasmic β-catenin positivity in spindle neoplastic cells, the characteristic immunophenotype of desmoid-type fibromatosis described in the caption and in-text.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical features of desmoid-type fibromatosis. (A) Low-power view (hematoxylin and eosin staining) shows a proliferation of uniform spindle cells arranged in long and intersecting fascicles dispersed in a dense collagenous stroma. (B) Higher magnification highlights spindle cells with elongated nuclei, displaying bland cytologic appearance. (C) Immunohistochemical staining for β-catenin reveals both strong cytoplasmic and nuclear positivity in neoplastic cells.
in_text_mentions: Histology demonstrated desmoid-type fibromatosis, characterized by fascicular proliferation of cytologically bland spindle cells within a dense collagenous stroma, with occasional mitotic figures and scattered mast cells. Peripheral infiltration of skeletal muscle was observed. Immunohistochemistry showed β-catenin and LEF1 (lymphoid enhancer-binding factor 1) positivity, focal desmin staining, and negativity for α-smooth-muscle actin, diffuse desmin, S-100, SOX10, broad-spectrum cytokeratins (MNF-116), and CD34 (Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Beta-catenin immunohistochemical stain of a biopsy from a 23-year-old male with extra-abdominal desmoid tumor (fibromatosis); the caption and in-text histology describe bland spindle cells in elongated fascicles, and the image shows diffusely positive beta-catenin staining with nuclear positivity, characteristic of desmoid fibromatosis.
panels.attribution_text: Boyett et al. Extra-abdominal Desmoid Tumor in a 23-Year-Old Male: A Case Report.. Cureus 2026. doi:10.7759/cureus.109286. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 6.
panels.figure_caption: Beta-catenin stain of the biopsy at 40x magnification. Beta-catenin stain of the biopsy demonstrating diffuse positive beta-catenin staining with extensive nuclear staining.
in_text_mentions: Muscle-specific actin had patchy areas of positive staining. Beta-catenin was diffusely positive and had extensive nuclear staining, as seen in Figure 6. Histology revealed soft tissue cores composed of bland spindle cells arranged in elongated fascicles with alternating areas of loose/myxoid and collagenous stroma. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H). A: H&E section shows classic desmoid tumor histology with sweeping fascicles of bland spindle cells in a collagenous stroma. B: H&E section shows classic desmoid tumor histology with sweeping fascicles of bland spindle cells in a collagenous stroma. C: Immunohistochemistry demonstrating strong nuclear β-catenin expression, supporting desmoid-type fibromatosis. D: Immunohistochemistry shows smooth muscle actin positivity, part of the desmoid tumor immunophenotype. E: Immunohistochemistry shows caldesmon positivity, consistent with the desmoid tumor immunophenotype. F: Immunohistochemistry shows cyclin D1 positivity, part of the desmoid tumor immunophenotype. G: Immunohistochemistry shows only focal/limited CD34 staining, consistent with desmoid tumor. H: Ki-67 immunohistochemistry shows a low proliferative index, typical of desmoid tumor.
panels.attribution_text: AlAnsari et al. Locally Aggressive Desmoid Tumor With L4-L5 Vertebral Invasion and Progressive Neurological Deficit: A Case Report.. Clinical case reports 2026. doi:10.1002/ccr3.73181. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.
panels.figure_caption: Histopathological and immunohistochemical findings of the pelvic mass. (A, B) Hematoxylin and eosin sections show a spindle‐cell neoplasm composed of bland fibroblastic/myofibroblastic cells arranged in sweeping fascicles within a collagenous stroma, without marked cytologic atypia. (C) Immunohistochemistry demonstrates strong nuclear β‐catenin expression, supporting desmoid‐type fibromatosis. (D–F) The tumor cells show immunoreactivity for smooth muscle actin, caldesmon, and cyclin D1. (G) CD34 staining is only focal/limited. (H) Ki‐67 shows a low proliferative index. The overall histomorphologic and immunohistochemical profile, together with CTNNB1 mutation analysis and absence of features supporting sarcoma or other spindle‐cell mimics, confirmed the diagnosis of desmoid‐type fibromatosis.
in_text_mentions: 9, BCL2, estrogen receptor, and ALK‐1 were negative. CD34 showed only focal faint positivity. Molecular analysis identified a likely pathogenic CTNNB1 p.(Ser45Pro) mutation with a high variant allele frequency, supporting activation of the Wnt/β‐catenin pathway. A pathogenic APC variant was also detected. In addition, fluorescence in situ hybridization showed no evidence of EWSR1 rearrangement, and further testing demonstrated no MDM2 amplification. Taken together, these histopathological, immunophenotypic, and molecular findings confirmed the diagnosis of desmoid‐type fibromatosis (Figure 2).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: HES overview of a core biopsy explicitly described as showing the characteristic architecture of desmoid-type fibromatosis in a 16-year-old patient with a right gluteal desmoid. B: Higher-magnification HES showing the sweeping fascicles of bland spindle cells in dense collagen typical of desmoid-type fibromatosis. C: Cellular detail of the bland spindle-cell proliferation without atypia or mitoses, consistent with desmoid fibromatosis in this biopsy. D: Beta-catenin immunohistochemistry on the same desmoid biopsy core, supporting desmoid-type fibromatosis in the appropriate histologic context. E: High-magnification beta-catenin immunolabeling of spindle cells supporting the diagnosis of desmoid-type fibromatosis. F: Ki-67 immunostain of the desmoid biopsy showing a low proliferation index, a feature of desmoid-type fibromatosis.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathology and immunohistochemistry of the right gluteal core-needle biopsy, October 2024. (A) HES, ×5: overview of the biopsy core showing a mildly cellular spindle-cell proliferation within an abundant collagenous stroma, with the characteristic architecture of desmoid-type fibromatosis. (B) HES, ×10: sweeping fascicles of bland fibroblastic spindle cells embedded in a dense collagenous background; no significant atypia or mitotic activity is identified. (C) HES, ×20: cellular detail confirming the absence of cytologic atypia and mitoses. (D) Beta-catenin immunohistochemistry, ×5: overview of the biopsy core showing beta-catenin labeling in spindle cells. (E) Beta-catenin, ×20: brown beta-catenin immunolabeling in spindle cells with hematoxylin counterstain, supporting the diagnosis of desmoid-type fibromatosis in the appropriate histologic context. (F) Ki-67, ×10: rare Ki-67-positive nuclei (brown) dispersed among a majority of negative cells, corresponding to a low proliferation index of 5%-10%. HES: Hematoxylin-eosin-saffron.
in_text_mentions: Image-guided core-needle biopsy of the right gluteal lesion confirmed desmoid-type fibromatosis with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 5%-10% (Figure 1). Genetic screening was negative for pathogenic APC mutations, supporting a sporadic presentation. Routine laboratory investigations were within normal limits.

in_text_mentions: but lack hyperchromasia. Intra-abdominal desmoids can sometimes contain relatively scanty collagen and a pronounced myxoid matrix. Spindle cells and collagen fibrils are usually arranged in ill-defined fascicles and interlacing bundles (Figs. 3, 4). Occasionally extensive glassy hyalinization, which is also a feature of keloid, may also be encountered. The tumors can vary in cellularity and may assume a more storiform architecture as well. Special stains such as reticulin and mason trichome have been traditionally used to highlight the collagen more clearly, but are currently rarely employed.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 6 panels (A, B, C, D, E, F). A: H&E low-power view of the pancreatic desmoid lesion showing a diffuse patchy fibrous proliferation with indistinct borders, consistent with the article diagnosis of aggressive fibromatosis/desmoid tumor. B: H&E panel showing residual pancreatic ducts within the desmoid lesion, supporting tumor involvement of the pancreas in this case. C: H&E panel showing dilated cystic pancreatic ducts within the desmoid lesion, a distinctive cystic feature of this pancreatic aggressive fibromatosis case. D: H&E panel demonstrating infiltrative spindle-shaped fibrous bundles invading the muscularis propria, characteristic of desmoid-type fibromatosis. E: H&E panel showing the desmoid lesion invading surrounding fibrofatty tissue, supporting the infiltrative nature of the tumor. F: High-magnification H&E panel showing the tumor cells to be fibroblasts and myofibroblasts, the characteristic cell population of desmoid-type fibromatosis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Sagittal pelvic MRI shows an enlarged presacral mass in a patient with desmoid tumor; the caption and article title support disease attribution. B: Axial T1-weighted fat-saturated MRI shows the enlarging pelvic desmoid and persistent right gluteal lesion, consistent with the captioned diagnosis. C: Axial T2-weighted MRI demonstrates a pelvic mass with internal hypointense fibrotic bands, explicitly described as typical of desmoid tumor.

panels.figure_caption: Follow-up pelvic MRI, June 2025. (A) Sagittal T2-weighted TSE image demonstrating the enlarged presacral pelvic mass with mass effect and displacement of the bladder, uterus, and rectum (arrows). (B) Axial T1-weighted volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination (VIBE) image with fat saturation showing marked interval enlargement of the pelvic mass and persistence of the right gluteal lesion (arrows). (C) Axial T2-weighted TSE image showing heterogeneous intermediate-to-high T2 signal intensity with internal hypointense fibrotic bands, typical of a desmoid tumor (arrow). VIBE: Volumetric interpolated breath-hold examination; TSE: Turbo spin-echo.
in_text_mentions: Follow-up pelvic MRI performed in June 2025 demonstrated marked interval enlargement of both lesions, with the pelvic component reaching approximately 130 × 95 mm and the gluteal lesion also progressing in size. T2 signal remained heterogeneous, with intermediate-to-high intensity relative to muscle and persistent hypointense fibrotic bands, in keeping with aggressive but biologically active fibromatosis (Figure 4).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: Gross resection specimen of a mesenteric desmoid tumor with a firm, trabeculated white cut surface and myxoid areas. B: H&E section shows the desmoid tumor infiltrating the small intestinal wall, consistent with the captioned mesenteric desmoid diagnosis. C: High-power H&E demonstrates bland spindle cells with collagenous stroma, typical histology of desmoid fibromatosis. D: Immunohistochemistry shows strong nuclear beta-catenin staining, supporting the diagnosis of desmoid tumor.

in_text_mentions: from the small intestine mesentery which tightly adhered to the surrounding organs. A cross-section revealed a glistening white, coarsely trabeculated surface, and myxoid appearance in some area (Fig. 3A). Microscopically, the lesion infiltrated the small intestine and colon wall (Fig. 3B). Bland spindle-shaped cells composed the tumor cytologically (Fig. 3C). Immunohistochemical staining showed strong nuclear β-catenin staining (Fig. 3D). These findings supported a diagnosis of mesenteric desmoid tumor. All resection margins were negative, which demonstrated a complete surgical excision (R0).

in_text_mentions: Contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT performed in February 2026 showed stable size of the dominant masses compared with the June 2025 MRI. However, new complications had developed: a large intravaginal hematoma (hematocolpos), a left pelvic fluid collection, and bilateral hydroureteronephrosis secondary to extrinsic ureteric compression by the pelvic mass. There was no evidence of bowel obstruction (Figure 5).

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: H&E low-power histology of the same desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis) tumor: bland spindle/fibroblast proliferation in a dense collagenous stroma infiltrating adjacent skeletal muscle, matching the captioned and in-text histomorphology. b: High-power H&E of the desmoid tumor showing uniform, well-differentiated spindle cells in collagenous stroma without atypia, as described in the caption and text. c: Low-power alpha-smooth muscle actin immunostain of the same desmoid tumor; focal cytoplasmic positivity is an ancillary immunophenotypic feature of fibromatosis but is not a specific named vocabulary finding, so no vocabulary finding is asserted. d: High-power alpha-smooth muscle actin immunostain of the desmoid tumor showing focal cytoplasmic positivity; supportive immunophenotype, with no specific vocabulary finding for this stain.

panels.figure_caption: Histopathologic examination of the tumor under low (a, x20) and high (b, x100) power magnification reveals a proliferation of well-differentiated fibroblasts within a collagenous stroma, with infiltration of (H&E stain). Immunohistochemistry shows focally positive cytoplasmic reaction for smooth muscle actin [immune-staining against smooth muscle actin (c, x40), (d, x400)].
in_text_mentions: Histopathologically, the lesion showed an increase in well-differentiated fibroblasts within a collagenous stroma with infiltration of nearby skeletal muscle and adipose tissues. The excision margins were negative, except for the area adjacent to the scalenus medius muscle. The cells did not show nuclear atypia or hyperchromasia (Figure 3a). Immunohistochemically, the tumor was negative for S-100, beta-catenin, and CD34 but focally positive for alpha-smooth muscle actin (Figure 3b). Based on the clinical behavior and histomorphological features, a definitive diagnosis of AF was made.

Clinical case reports 2026. doi:10.1002/ccr3.73328. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: (A) Non‐contrast coronal abdominopelvic CT image demonstrating a large, infiltrative mesenteric mass (between white arrows) in the lower abdomen and pelvis, consistent with a desmoid tumor. The mass infiltrates the greater omentum, displaces small bowel loops, invades the right ureter, and compresses the left ureter, leading to moderate bilateral hydroureteronephrosis. (B) Non‐contrast axial abdominopelvic CT image, the mass is seen encasing and invading the right ureter (white arrow). (C) Non‐contrast axial abdominopelvic CT image demonstrating bilateral hydroureteronephrosis (black arrows), with visible dilation of both renal pelvicalyceal systems and proximal ureters. The findings are consistent with obstructive uropathy, attributed to an infiltrative mesenteric desmoid tumor encasing and compressing the ureters. (D) Non‐contrast axial abdominopelvic CT image showing post‐surgical changes consistent with prior total colectomy, including absence of colonic structures and evidence of stoma placement (black arrow) in the right abdominal wall. A large, ill‐defined desmoid tumor measuring approximately 11 × 7 × 12 cm is seen occupying the lower abdomen and pelvic cavity, with infiltration and displacement of adjacent small bowel loops (red arrow) and involvement of the right ureter, contributing to obstructive pyelonephritis. Additionally, a well‐defined, subcutaneous, 1 × 1 × 1 cm soft tissue lesion is noted in the posterior midline over the sacral region (white arrow), suggestive of a subcutaneous epidermoid cyst.
in_text_mentions: soft‐tissue mass measuring approximately 11 × 7 × 12 cm was identified in the lower abdomen and pelvic cavity, likely of mesenteric origin, and was consistent with a desmoid‐type fibromatosis (Figure 1A). The mass displaces adjacent small bowel loops, compresses the right ureter (Figure 1B), and compresses the left ureter, resulting in moderate bilateral hydronephrosis (Figure 1C). No intratumoral calcifications or necrosis were identified. panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: H&E histology of resected desmoid tumor showing bland spindle cells, consistent with the article diagnosis. B: Beta-catenin immunohistochemistry of the resected desmoid tumor, showing the characteristic cytoplasmic and nuclear positivity described in the caption. in_text_mentions: ped by the known infiltrative nodule. Macroscopically, this lesion was bigger than expected, with an estimated diameter of 60 mm. The lesion was solid, firm, and infiltrative, surrounding the ureter (Figure 2), right iliac vessels, and hypogastric nerve. Also, it infiltrated the right parametrium. We did an incisional biopsy for an intraoperative diagnosis. On frozen section, a descriptive diagnosis of a nonspecific, bland fusiform cell lesion, with no cytological atypia and associated dense collagenated stroma, was established. An epithelial malignancy or endometriosis was excluded. Also, dur

amination, the lesion consisted of an infiltrative, fibroelastic tumor that measured approximately 5 cm on the long axis, with a white, whorled appearance and ill-defined borders, on the cut surface (Figure 2). The lesion, macroscopically, seemed to compress the adjacent ureter. Microscopically, the tumor was composed by an infiltrative growth pattern proliferation of bland spindle cells, arranged in long fascicles, with fusiform, uniform, nuclei, and inconspicuous nucleoli, with no cytological atypia, in a stroma with bundles of collagen (Figure 3). There were no mitoses or necrosis observed.

panels.figure_caption: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans conducted on the upper back region There is a notable mass observed within the rhomboid muscles (write arrows), encompassing both the minor and major parts. This lesion demonstrates hyperintensity on T2-Weighted (T2W) images. In post-contrast images, the mass reveals a homogeneous strong enhancement. The lesion exhibits invasive characteristics, with evidence of infiltration into the longissimus cervicis muscle (red arrows) and the infraspinatus muscle (blue arrows). The MRI features are suggestive of a desmoid tumor in the rhomboid muscles with invasion into the longissimus cervicis and infraspinatus muscles.
in_text_mentions: Due to persistent pain and the detected mass, the chiropractor prescribed a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan for the upper back region, which revealed the presence of an intramuscular lesion of 8 × 4 cm. This lesion was found to penetrate the cervical area of the right rhomboid muscle, without any involvement of the superficial subcutaneous tissues or the skin (Figure 2). Detection of the mass posed a diagnostic challenge as the initial symptoms were suggestive of myofascial pain syndrome, emphasizing the importance of a thorough physical examination.

A: Grayscale ultrasound of the duodenal aggressive fibromatosis (desmoid tumor) mass in a human patient; caption and in-text explicitly attribute the lesion to AF in this case report. B: Color Doppler ultrasound of the same desmoid (aggressive fibromatosis) mass showing the lesion with scant internal vascularity. in_text_mentions: EA) level every 3 months and computed tomography (CT) and/or ultrasonography every 6 months. At 27 months after gastrectomy, an increase in serum CEA level was detected during follow up (Figure 1). CT and positron emission tomography (PET) were subsequently performed. CT revealed a solitary, localized mass measuring 15 mm in diameter in the mesentery of the transverse colon (Figure 2a). Radiotracer fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake of this tumor was seen (Figure 2b) during the PET study. The maximum standard uptake value (SUV max) of the early phase was 3.86, and that of the late phase was 2.87.

ered that this tumor was a recurrence, in the lymph node or peritoneum, of the previous gastric cancer. We initiated first-line chemotherapy consisting of cisplatin and S-1 for five cycles. Serum CEA levels slightly decreased (Figure 1). However, no clinical response was observed in image inspections (Figure 2c, d); the tumor was noted to have slightly enlarged, but no new lesions were observed. Because curative resection seemed possible, we decided to completely resect the tumor. The tumor strongly adhered to the transverse colon; therefore, this part of the transverse colon was also removed.

Duodenal location is unusual/rare for desmoid tumor. B: Human patient contrast-enhanced CT showing the same duodenal soft tissue mass; caption attributes the mass to the patient's desmoid tumor. C: Human gastroscopy image showing a significant duodenal bulge due to the desmoid tumor; no direct desmoid-specific vocabulary finding applies. D: Human gastroscopy image showing luminal narrowing/obstruction from the duodenal desmoid tumor; no direct desmoid-specific vocabulary finding applies. E: Human ultrasound image showing a hypoechoic mass outside the descending duodenal wall, consistent with the patient's desmoid tumor; arrow annotates the mass.

A: Non-enhanced axial CT of a patient with intestinal aggressive fibromatosis (desmoid tumor); caption describes a well-demarcated hypodense left abdominal mass, a specific manifestation of the target disease. B: Arterial-phase axial CT of the same desmoid tumor, showing mild heterogeneous enhancement of the left abdominal mass. C: Portal venous phase axial CT demonstrating progressive enhancement of the desmoid mass, a characteristic feature. D: Delayed equilibrium phase axial CT of the desmoid tumor showing further enhancement, completing the progressive enhancement pattern. E: Axial T1-weighted MRI of the desmoid tumor showing the soft tissue mass with isointense solid and low-signal cystic components. panels.figure_caption: CT and MRI findings of aggressive fibromatosis at the splenic flexure of the colon. (A–D) Axial CT images. (A) Non-enhanced CT shows a well-demarcated, slightly hypodense mass in the left abdomen with surrounding exudative changes. (B) Arterial phase image demonstrates mild heterogeneous enhancement of the lesion. (C) Portal venous phase image reveals progressive enhancement. (D) On delayed equilibrium phase imaging, further increase in enhancement is observed, consistent with a progressive enhancement pattern. (E–L) MR images. (E) T1WI: the solid component of the mass is isointense to muscle, while the cystic portion shows low signal intensity. (F) T2WI: the solid component is slightly hyperintense, and the cystic areas show heterogeneous high signal. (G) DWI (b=800 s/mm2): the cystic component exhibits high signal intensity, whereas the solid part remains isointense. (H) ADC map: corresponding low signal in the cystic regions confirms restricted diffusion; the solid component is isointense. (I) Arterial phase: mild heterogeneous enhancement of the solid tumor. (J) Portal venous phase: increased enhancement. (K) Venous phase: persistent enhancement, with the cyst wall and septa 467 demonstrating marked enhancement. Tumor rupture with communication to the peritoneal cavity 468 is noted (red arrow). (L) Delayed phase (coronal): marked enhancement of the lesion; note 469 secondary upper gastrointestinal obstruction with gastric and proximal duodenal dilatation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (a, b, c, d). a: Sagittal T2-weighted pelvic MRI shows a round pelvic mass with low central T2 signal in a patient with desmoid tumor. b: Sagittal postgadolinium T1-weighted fat-suppressed MRI shows a pelvic desmoid tumor with heterogeneous/minimal enhancement typical of fibrous tissue. c: Paracoronal T2-weighted MRI shows right hydronephrosis due to ureteral obstruction attributed in the caption to a desmoid tumor; hydronephrosis is not in the vocabulary. d: Postgadolinium T1-weighted MRI shows right hydronephrosis from extraureteral obstruction confirmed to be due to desmoid tumor; hydronephrosis is not in the vocabulary.
panels.attribution_text: Ormonde et al. Pelvic Desmoid Tumor: A Rare Case with Difficult Diagnosis and Treatment.. Case reports in obstetrics and gynecology 2022. doi:10.1155/2022/7653246. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging showing the following: (a) sagittal T2-weighted spin-echo image: a round mass with very low homogeneous signal intensity in its central part is present; (b) sagittal 90 second postgadolinium T1-weighted fat-suppressed spin-echo image: the upper aspect of the mass enhances reflecting active disease and the nodular desmoid tumor exhibits minimal enhancement confirming its fibrous nature; (c) paracoronal T2-weighted; and (d) postgadolinium T1-weighted images showing right kidney hydronephrosis due to an extraureteral obstruction confirmed to be a desmoid tumor.
